title: Change of Basis
---

What happens to the matrix of a linear map when we choose different bases? Let $\mathcal{B} = (v_1, \ldots, v_n)$ and $\mathcal{B}' = (v_1', \ldots, v_n')$ be two bases of $V$, the “old” and the “new” one. Write each new basis vector in terms of the old basis: $$v'_j = \sum_{i=1}^{n} p_{ij} v_i.$$

:::definition{5.3.1} Change-of-basis matrix
The $n \times n$ matrix $P = (p_{ij})$, whose $j$-th column is the coordinate vector of $v_j'$ in the old basis $\mathcal{B}$, is the ***change-of-basis matrix*** from $\mathcal{B}'$ to $\mathcal{B}$. Comparing with the definition of the matrix of a linear map, $$P = \mcM(\id_V, \mathcal{B}', \mathcal{B}),$$ the matrix of the identity map of $V$ with the new basis used in the domain and the old basis in the target.
:::

Symbolically, $$(v_1' \; \cdots \; v_n') = (v_1 \; \cdots \; v_n)P, \qquad \text{so} \qquad (v_1' \; \cdots \; v_n')X' = (v_1 \; \cdots \; v_n)PX'.$$ In words:

:::proposition{5.3.2} Change of coordinates
If a vector has coordinate vector $X'$ in the new basis $\mathcal{B}'$, then its coordinate vector in the old basis $\mathcal{B}$ is $X = PX'$. The matrix $P$ is invertible, with inverse $P^{-1} = \mcM(\id_V, \mathcal{B}, \mathcal{B}')$, and $X' = P^{-1}X$.
:::

:::proof
The first statement is Proposition [5.2.4](/notes/math-55a/5-2-matrices-of-linear-maps#proposition-5-2-4) applied to $\id_V$, with the basis $\mathcal{B}'$ in the domain and $\mathcal{B}$ in the target. By Proposition [5.2.9](/notes/math-55a/5-2-matrices-of-linear-maps#proposition-5-2-9), $$\mcM(\id_V, \mathcal{B}', \mathcal{B})\,\mcM(\id_V, \mathcal{B}, \mathcal{B}') = \mcM(\id_V, \mathcal{B}, \mathcal{B}) = I_n,$$ and likewise in the other order.
:::

Note the direction: $P$ has the *new* basis vectors as its columns, but it converts *new* coordinates into *old* ones.

:::theorem{5.3.3} Change of basis
Let $\varphi : V \to W$ be linear, let $\mathcal{B}, \mathcal{B}'$ be bases of $V$ and $\mathcal{C}, \mathcal{C}'$ bases of $W$, and put $$A = \mcM(\varphi, \mathcal{B}, \mathcal{C}), \qquad P = \mcM(\id_V, \mathcal{B}', \mathcal{B}), \qquad Q = \mcM(\id_W, \mathcal{C}, \mathcal{C}').$$ Then $\mcM(\varphi, \mathcal{B}', \mathcal{C}') = QAP$.
:::

:::proof
Write $\varphi = \id_W \circ \varphi \circ \id_V$ and apply Proposition [5.2.9](/notes/math-55a/5-2-matrices-of-linear-maps#proposition-5-2-9), using the bases $\mathcal{B}' \to \mathcal{B} \to \mathcal{C} \to \mathcal{C}'$: $$\mcM(\varphi, \mathcal{B}', \mathcal{C}') = \mcM(\id_W, \mathcal{C}, \mathcal{C}')\,\mcM(\varphi, \mathcal{B}, \mathcal{C})\,\mcM(\id_V, \mathcal{B}', \mathcal{B}) = QAP.$$ In the symbolic notation, with $(w_1 \; \cdots \; w_m) = (w_1' \; \cdots \; w_m')Q$: $$\begin{aligned}
\varphi\big((v_1' \; \cdots \; v_n')X'\big) &= \varphi\big((v_1 \; \cdots \; v_n)PX'\big) \\
&= (w_1 \; \cdots \; w_m)APX' = (w_1' \; \cdots \; w_m')QAPX'.
\end{aligned}$$
:::

Here $Q$ is the inverse of the change-of-basis matrix from $\mathcal{C}'$ to $\mathcal{C}$. The most important case is an operator, with the same basis used on both sides.

:::corollary{5.3.4} Change of basis for operators
Let $\varphi \in \End(V)$, let $\mathcal{B}$ and $\mathcal{B}'$ be bases of $V$, and let $P = \mcM(\id_V, \mathcal{B}', \mathcal{B})$. If $A = \mcM(\varphi, \mathcal{B})$ and $A' = \mcM(\varphi, \mathcal{B}')$, then $$A' = P^{-1}AP.$$
:::

:::proof
Apply the theorem with $W = V$, $\mathcal{C} = \mathcal{B}$ and $\mathcal{C}' = \mathcal{B}'$. Then $Q = \mcM(\id_V, \mathcal{B}, \mathcal{B}') = P^{-1}$ by Proposition [5.3.2](/notes/math-55a/5-3-change-of-basis#proposition-5-3-2).
:::

So the matrices representing the *same* linear operator in different bases are related by ***conjugation*** by an invertible matrix. Still, the whole point of linear algebra is to work with linear maps in coordinate-free language as much as possible, and to choose bases only when they make a computation transparent.

## <span class="num">5.3.1</span> Similar Matrices

:::definition{5.3.5} Similar matrices
Two matrices $A, B \in \mathcal{M}_n(k)$ are ***similar***, written $A \sim B$, if there exists an invertible matrix $P \in \GL_n(k)$ such that $$B = P^{-1}AP.$$
:::

:::proposition{5.3.6} Similarity is an equivalence relation
Similarity is an equivalence relation on $\mathcal{M}_n(k)$.
:::

:::proof
It is reflexive: $A = I^{-1}AI$. It is symmetric: if $B = P^{-1}AP$, then $A = PBP^{-1} = (P^{-1})^{-1}B(P^{-1})$. It is transitive: if $B = P^{-1}AP$ and $C = Q^{-1}BQ$, then $C = Q^{-1}P^{-1}APQ = (PQ)^{-1}A(PQ)$.
:::

:::proposition{5.3.7} Similar matrices represent the same operator
Two matrices $A, B \in \mathcal{M}_n(k)$ are similar if and only if there are an $n$-dimensional space $V$, an operator $\varphi \in \End(V)$ and bases $\mathcal{B}, \mathcal{B}'$ of $V$ with $A = \mcM(\varphi, \mathcal{B})$ and $B = \mcM(\varphi, \mathcal{B}')$.
:::

:::proof
If $A$ and $B$ are matrices of one operator in two bases, they are similar by Corollary [5.3.4](/notes/math-55a/5-3-change-of-basis#corollary-5-3-4). Conversely, suppose $B = P^{-1}AP$. Take $V = k^n$ and $\varphi = L_A$, whose matrix in the standard basis $\mathcal{E}$ is $A$. The columns of $P$ form a basis $\mathcal{B}'$ of $k^n$ by Proposition [5.2.14](/notes/math-55a/5-2-matrices-of-linear-maps#proposition-5-2-14), and $P = \mcM(\id, \mathcal{B}', \mathcal{E})$ because its columns are the vectors of $\mathcal{B}'$ written in the standard basis. By the corollary, $\mcM(L_A, \mathcal{B}') = P^{-1}AP = B$.
:::

So a similarity class of $n \times n$ matrices records exactly what one operator looks like in all possible bases. A property of matrices that is unchanged by similarity, a ***similarity invariant***, is therefore a property of the operator itself, shared by all the matrices that represent it. We now meet the first such invariant, the trace; the determinant follows in Section [5.4](/notes/math-55a/5-4-determinants).

## <span class="num">5.3.2</span> The Trace

:::definition{5.3.8} Trace of a matrix
The ***trace*** of a square matrix $A = (a_{ij}) \in \mathcal{M}_n(k)$ is the sum of its diagonal entries: $$\Tr(A) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} a_{ii} = a_{11} + a_{22} + \cdots + a_{nn}.$$
:::

The trace is a linear map $\mathcal{M}_n(k) \to k$.

:::lemma{5.3.9} Cyclic property of the trace
If $A \in \mathcal{M}_{m \times n}(k)$ and $B \in \mathcal{M}_{n \times m}(k)$, then $\Tr(AB) = \Tr(BA)$.
:::

:::proof
We have $$\Tr(AB) = \sum_{i=1}^{m} (AB)_{ii} = \sum_{i=1}^{m} \sum_{j=1}^{n} a_{ij} b_{ji}, \qquad \Tr(BA) = \sum_{j=1}^{n} (BA)_{jj} = \sum_{j=1}^{n} \sum_{i=1}^{m} b_{ji} a_{ij}.$$ These are the same finite sum, taken in two different orders.
:::

:::proposition{5.3.10} Trace is a similarity invariant
If $A \sim B$, then $\Tr(A) = \Tr(B)$.
:::

:::proof
If $B = P^{-1}AP$, then by the cyclic property applied to $P^{-1}A$ and $P$, $$\Tr(B) = \Tr\big((P^{-1}A)P\big) = \Tr\big(P(P^{-1}A)\big) = \Tr(A).$$
:::

:::definition{5.3.11} Trace of an operator
Let $V$ be finite-dimensional. The ***trace*** of an operator $\varphi \in \End(V)$ is $$\Tr(\varphi) = \Tr\big(\mcM(\varphi, \mathcal{B})\big)$$ for any basis $\mathcal{B}$ of $V$. It does not depend on $\mathcal{B}$: by Corollary [5.3.4](/notes/math-55a/5-3-change-of-basis#corollary-5-3-4) the matrices of $\varphi$ in two bases are similar, and similar matrices have the same trace.
:::

:::proposition{5.3.12} Properties of the trace
Let $V$ be finite-dimensional, $\varphi, \psi \in \End(V)$ and $\lambda \in k$. Then $\Tr(\varphi + \psi) = \Tr(\varphi) + \Tr(\psi)$, $\Tr(\lambda\varphi) = \lambda\Tr(\varphi)$, $\Tr(\varphi \circ \psi) = \Tr(\psi \circ \varphi)$, and $\Tr(\id_V) = \dim V \cdot 1$.
:::

:::proof
Fix a basis and take matrices. The map $\varphi \mapsto \mcM(\varphi)$ is a ring isomorphism (Corollary [5.2.10](/notes/math-55a/5-2-matrices-of-linear-maps#corollary-5-2-10)), the trace of matrices is linear, $\Tr(AB) = \Tr(BA)$ by Lemma [5.3.9](/notes/math-55a/5-3-change-of-basis#lemma-5-3-9), and $\mcM(\id_V) = I_n$ has trace $n \cdot 1$.
:::

:::note
In Chapter 9 the trace of an operator is described without any choice of basis, as a contraction of tensors; that description makes its basis-independence evident.
:::
